questions.headline: No data row is dropped — the only filter removes fully blank lines, and none exist; the header is validated, not counted as data. The difference is 0 for all three extracts, and the manifest keeps both numbers so a future drop cannot go unnoticed.
questions.method: `load_raw` parses every file with `csv.reader` and returns `(header, rows)`; `write_manifest` records `rows_in_file` and `rows_loaded` from that same pass, so the comparison is like-for-like per table.

result.value: customers 520 = 520; products 30 = 30; orders 6,103 = 6,103; blank lines skipped 0; rows delivered to cleaning 6,103.

questions.title: Rows per extract vs rows loaded

questions.headline: Column names are kept exactly as the extract writes them — no rename at load. A mismatch is fail-fast, never a silent mapping, so if a source renames a column the pipeline stops instead of guessing at the data.
questions.method: `load_raw` compares each file header to `EXPECTED_HEADERS[table]` and raises `ValueError` on mismatch; `write_manifest` stores the header verbatim for audit.

result.value: headers match exactly 3/3 — customers (6 columns), products (5), orders (11); odd names found: none; each header recorded verbatim in the manifest.

questions.title: Odd column names kept verbatim

questions.headline: Text is the preservation layer and coercion happens only in the normalisation helpers (`parse_float`, `parse_int`, `parse_date`, `parse_discount_frac`), so leading zeros, currency symbols, '%' and mixed date formats can never be mangled by dtype guessing. Disagreeing columns (a naive typed read would change them): orders — `order_id` (leading zeros `O00007`), `customer_id`/`product_id` (case/dash/space variants), `order_date` (mixed formats), `quantity` (`-2`, `''`, `2.5`), `unit_price_paid` (rupee-symbol forms, `NA`), `discount` (`10%`, `15`, `20 percent`, `NA`), `delivery_days`, `payment_mode`, `order_status`; customers — `customer_id`, `phone` (111 values start with `0`), `signup_date`; products — `product_id`, `unit_price` (`₹60`, `1,200`, `NA`), `stock_qty` (`NA`).
questions.method: The loader keeps every cell as text (csv module, list-of-dicts; `dtype=str, keep_default_na=False` when profiling), so no type inference happens at load; a typed read was compared column-by-column on the raw forms to list where inference would disagree.

result.value: quantity texts: `-2` x111, `0` x251, `2.5` x62, blank x170; discount has 7 distinct forms (`0`, `NA`, `5%`, `15`, `20 percent`, `10%`, `0.1`); rupee sign x128 across files (125 order prices, 3 product prices); phone leading zeros preserved x111; all values survive load unchanged.

questions.title: Numeric-looking text columns

questions.headline: No short or long rows exist — the standard CSV quoting rules inside `csv.reader` keep every logical row intact. The audit is a permanent guard: a malformed row cannot pass unnoticed in future loads.
questions.method: `row_length_audit` counts fields per parsed row and the manifest stores the distribution per table; a row broken by quoting would show a length different from its header.

result.value: customers {6: 520}, products {5: 30}, orders {11: 6,103}; short rows 0, long rows 0; quoting-caused splits 0.

questions.title: Short/long order rows

questions.headline: Raw ids stay verbatim in the extracts (audit trail) and joins use `norm_id` — variants like `C-0176` and `c0010` resolve without editing the source. Leading zeros survive because values are text; nothing is integerised.
questions.method: Id values carrying spaces, lower case or dashes are counted per column; `norm_id` (strip, UPPER, remove spaces/dashes) shows the canonical form. One example per class demonstrates preservation at load and canonicalisation at join time.

result.value: trailing-space ids 8 (`C0032 `, `C0140 `, `C0203 `), lower-case ids 19 (`c0010`), dash ids 4 (`C-0176`, `C-0197`, `C-0308`, `C-0445`), rows changed by normalisation 23, distinct ids 500 before = 500 after. (Orders): `customer_id` — 94 rows with spaces (`C0140 `), 476 lower case (`c0108`), 38 dashed; `product_id` — 1,019 dashed (`P-21`), 178 lower case (`p09`); `order_id` — 0 variants (all `O0####`, leading zeros kept). Examples: `norm_id('C-0176') = 'C0176'`; `norm_id(' p09 ') = 'P09'`.

questions.title: Leading zeros and spaces in ids

questions.headline: Day-first conventions are tried before month-first (`%d/%m/%Y` precedes `%m/%d/%Y`), so ambiguous strings follow the Indian convention — raw `01/11/2026` is read day-first as 1 Nov 2026 (visible in `quality_datamart` row O00004). Unparseable dates are quarantined, never guessed.
questions.method: `parse_date` tries the ordered 8-format list and then an ISO fallback; counts compare raw strings against their parsed ISO form to separate changed values from unparseable ones.

result.value: already ISO 1,151; changed 4,662; unparseable 290 (QC_ORD_DATE_INVALID). Main changed families: DD/MM/YYYY 2,290, DD.MM.YYYY 1,237, DD-Mon-YY (98–116 per month token, all 12 present). (customers, 520): already ISO 108; changed 387; unparseable 25 (QC_CUST_SIGNUP_UNPARSEABLE).

questions.title: Dates changed on load

questions.headline: UTF-8 is tried before cp1252, so the rupee sign decodes correctly; cp1252 stays only as a legacy fallback. No accent misreads are possible here (none exist), and `parse_float` defensively strips the rupee sign and commas so decoded symbol forms still parse.
questions.method: `detect_encoding` checks a UTF-8 BOM, then strict UTF-8, falling back to cp1252; a byte-level scan lists every non-ASCII character per file, and a misread test decodes bytes as cp1252.

result.value: all three files decode as plain UTF-8 (no BOM); non-ASCII: customers 0, products 3 x `₹`, orders 125 x `₹` (all in `unit_price_paid`); accents 0. Misread test: read as cp1252, each `₹` (3 UTF-8 bytes) becomes `â‚¹` mojibake — 125 garbled prices in orders.csv; the UTF-8-first policy prevents that.

questions.title: File encodings

questions.headline: Embedded commas and quotes are handled by standard CSV quoting (`""` escaping) rather than custom splitting, and the row-length audit proves no affected row misaligned.
questions.method: `csv.reader` handles quoting; the check counts notes containing commas or double quotes and re-audits row lengths — a quoting failure shows up as a wrong field count.

result.value: notes with commas 2,141; notes with double quotes 545; notes empty 2,265; rows with a wrong field count 0 (all 6,103 rows exactly 11 fields) — no row split or merged by quoting.

questions.title: Quotes inside notes

questions.headline: Extracts are immutable, content-addressed inputs: the manifest pins file, SHA-256, encoding, header and row counts, and reloading is idempotent — same bytes give same rows and same hash. Reruns therefore reproduce identical state; there is no sampling or randomness anywhere in loading.
questions.method: `load_raw` was run twice per extract and `sha256_of` twice per file in one session; row counts and hashes were compared (live demonstration, not a by-construction claim).

result.value: load1 == load2 rows: 520 / 30 / 6,103; SHA-256 stable: customers `fce10dec...`, products `a0878195...`, orders `03a9482a...` (full hashes in `data/raw_manifest.json`).

questions.title: Loading the same file twice

questions.headline: A placeholder is not a value — it is treated exactly like an empty cell by every downstream rule and profile, and only its count is kept so a badly supplied column stays visible. "Missing" means empty + placeholder everywhere in this project.
questions.method: `is_missing_or_placeholder` separates empty cells from the 16-token placeholder set (`NA`, `N/A`, `-`, `--`, `unknown`, `null`, `None`, `?`, `MISSING` and case variants); counts are produced per customer column.

result.value: customer_id 0/0; customer_name 20/0; email 32/10 (=42 missing, matches `profile.csv`); city 39/0; phone 109/0; signup_date 11/14 (=25). QC cross-checks: name 20, email 57 invalid (incl. malformed), city 39, signup 25, id duplicates 40 rows.

questions.title: Empty vs placeholder cells per customer column

questions.headline: Placeholders exist in only three columns — `discount` 576, `order_date` 110, `unit_price_paid` 68 — and missingness is spread across the whole timeline (no month holds more than 6.3% of any column's missing values). There is no process-fault window; this reads as sporadic entry omission, handled per column with reported coverage, not by excluding months.
questions.method: Per-column empty vs placeholder counts come from the raw extract; missing values are then bucketed by order month and the worst month's share of each column's missing total is measured.

result.value: order_date 180 empty + 110 placeholder (=290); unit_price_paid 199+68 (=267); discount 551+576 (=1,127); payment_mode 564 empty; order_status 629; delivery_days 142; notes 2,265; customer_id 60; product_id 54; quantity 170. Clustering (missing, month-buckets, worst month): unit_price_paid 267 over 49, max 12 (4.5%); discount 1,127 over 62, max 60 (5.3%); payment_mode 564 over 53, max 28 (5.0%); order_status 629 over 52, max 32 (5.1%); delivery_days 142 over 40, max 9 (6.3%); notes 2,265 over 76, max 99 (4.4%); order_date — 290 unparseable, so no month bucket is possible.

questions.title: Placeholders in orders and their clustering

questions.headline: `notes` is the most-empty column at 37.11%, but its emptiness is uniform across statuses (35–39% each) — it is an optional free-text field, not a workflow signal. `delivery_days` is equally status-independent (missing in Delivered rows too), so KPI scope simply excludes missing cells and reports coverage.
questions.method: Missing share per orders column is read from `profile.csv`; the two plausibly workflow-driven columns (`notes`, `delivery_days`) are then compared across statuses as within-status shares.

result.value: notes 2,265 (37.11%) > discount 1,127 (18.47%) > order_status 629 (10.31%) > payment_mode 564 (9.24%) > order_date 290 (4.75%) > unit_price_paid 267 (4.37%) > quantity 170 (2.79%) > delivery_days 142 (2.33%) > customer_id 60 (0.98%) > product_id 54 (0.88%) > order_id 0. Notes-empty by status: Delivered 655/1,803 (36.3%), Cancelled 709/1,828 (38.8%), In transit 223/602 (37.0%), Pending 237/623 (38.0%), Returned 220/618 (35.6%), blank status 221/629 (35.1%).

questions.title: Most-empty orders column

questions.headline: No month or product carries an unusual share — the worst month holds 12 (4.5%) and the worst product 14 (5.2%) of the 267 empties, near the uniform expectation (~8.9 per product). The one pattern worth noting: 11 empties sit in rows whose order_date is also unusable — both fields absent together.
questions.method: The 267 empty `unit_price_paid` cells are bucketed by order month and by product_id to see how the empties spread across the calendar and catalogue.
questions.title: Empty prices by month/product

questions.headline: The 57 flagged rows are 42 missing/placeholder plus 15 malformed. Placeholders are excluded from contactability rather than imputed, and malformed addresses are quarantined — no email is guessed or derived; normalised email (lower, strip) is used only for D03 identity matching.
questions.method: Emails are split into two groups — missing/placeholder (empty or a placeholder token) and format-invalid (non-empty, non-placeholder, failing the `@` rule) — and reconciled against the QC count.

result.value: missing 42 (32 empty + 10 placeholder, e.g. `N/A`); malformed 15 (e.g. `arjunshettymail.com` without `@`); flagged total 57; usable 463; placeholder share of flagged 10.

questions.title: Missing and placeholder emails

questions.headline: Four prices are written in text form — `₹60` (P-10), `₹210` (P13, P25), `1,200` (P21) — and all parse once the symbol/comma is stripped, so they are usable. The two `NA` values stay null and are the only QC failures; price comparisons run on the 28 parseable prices with coverage noted.
questions.method: The 30 catalogue `unit_price` values are classified as plain number, numeric-with-text-form (rupee sign or thousands separator), or unusable (`NA`/blank); QC_PROD_PRICE_INVALID is the cross-check.

result.value: non-numeric texts 6 = text forms 4 (`₹60`, `₹210`, `₹210`, `1,200`) + unusable 2 (`NA`: P-26 Apple Juice 1L, P-30 Honey 500g); QC failures 2; pass 28.

questions.title: Missing and text prices

questions.headline: Identifier columns are complete, so joins and row counts are safe. Each >10% column limits one specific analysis — phone (contactability), stock_qty (stock reports), discount (read as "no discount"), order_status (segment coverage), notes (free text) — and must be scoped to non-missing cells with coverage stated, never silently defaulted.
questions.method: `profile.csv` missing shares are scanned for columns at exactly 0% and above 10%, across all three tables.

result.value: never-empty — orders.order_id (6,103), customers.customer_id (520), products.product_id and products.product_name (30). Above 10% missing — stock_qty 40.00%, notes 37.11%, phone 20.96%, discount 18.47%, order_status 10.31% (payment_mode 9.24% just below; order_date 4.75%).

questions.title: Never-empty vs >10% empty columns

questions.headline: The 142 empties (2.33%) are spread evenly — every status sits between 1.8% and 3.9%, including `Delivered` — so no status explains them and nothing is learnt from status. Delivery-time metrics use the 5,961 rows with a value; the pattern says entry omission, not a workflow rule (cancelled orders are not the cause).
questions.method: Empty `delivery_days` values are grouped by order_status (raw spellings) and converted to within-status shares so statuses of different sizes compare fairly.
questions.title: Empty delivery days by status

questions.headline: The strongest pairs all involve optional fields (discount, notes, status, payment) going missing together, and required fields never co-miss in a material pair — one cause explains the tail: rows captured with minimal information leave optional cells blank together. No systemic capture fault needs modelling.
questions.method: Pair-wise co-emptiness is counted over all order columns (missing = empty or placeholder) and ranked by pair count.

result.value: top pairs — discount+notes 408, order_status+notes 221, payment_mode+notes 218, discount+order_status 128, discount+payment_mode 104, notes+order_date 99, unit_price_paid+notes 88, discount+order_date 60 (single-column totals: notes 2,265; discount 1,127; status 629; payment 564).

questions.title: Co-empty column pairs

questions.headline: 14 of 30 products (46.7%) lack usable stock, so a stock report covers only 16 products; category roll-ups are partial (Beverages 0/3 usable) and must publish coverage — an overall stock total would understate and should not be produced.
questions.method: `stock_qty` is classified per product (usable number vs missing vs negative/non-integer) and rolled up per category with spelling variants grouped; QC_PROD_STOCK_INVALID is the cross-check.

result.value: usable 16, unusable 14 (missing 12 + negative/non-integer 2). Per category: Grocery 7/10 usable (3 missing), Snacks 4/9 (4 missing, 1 bad), Beverages 0/3 (2 missing, 1 bad), Dairy & Eggs 2/4, Dairy 1/2, Household 1/1, missing category 1/1.

questions.title: Unusable stock per category

questions.headline: Every repeat is an exact copy on all business columns — there are no non-exact copies to review (conflicts 0). The D02 reviewer path exists (priority survivor: Delivered > In Transit > Pending > Returned > Cancelled > missing) but is unexercised; repeats span all statuses, marking them as system double-writes rather than one workflow stage.
questions.method: Order-id repeats are counted on the raw extract; each repeat group is tested for conflicting business values (the D02 case), and the duplicate registry shows what the pipeline removed (D01).

result.value: repeated order_ids 103; rows involved 206; conflicting groups 0; D01 removals 103; QC_ORD_ID_DUP flags 206 rows; removed-copy statuses (cleaned): Delivered 34, Cancelled 30, Pending 14, Returned 10, In Transit 9, MISSING 6 (the cleaned marker for a blank raw status).

questions.title: Repeated order_ids

questions.headline: No column differs — not even order_id or notes — so the duplicates are byte-identical copies (capture errors/double-writes). A correction would appear as one order_id with differing values (D02); there are none, so keep-first removal never discards edited data.
questions.method: Within each of the 103 duplicate groups, the number of distinct values is counted per column (all business columns and order_id), so any differing column would appear with a non-zero frequency.

result.value: per-column difference frequencies — order_id 0; customer_id 0; product_id 0; order_date 0; quantity 0; unit_price_paid 0; discount 0; payment_mode 0; order_status 0; delivery_days 0; notes 0.

questions.title: Which columns differ across copies

questions.headline: Same normalised email = same person even when id/case/spacing differ; survivor = earliest signup_date (tie: lower customer_id), and loser ids remap in orders before order-level dedup. Kept: 520 rows → 499 master rows (21 merged away).
questions.method: D03 groups customers by normalised email (lower, strip; placeholders never merge), keeps the earliest signup as survivor, and records every loser with its evidence; counts are rebuilt from the registry.

result.value: merges 21 = 20 same-id repeat registrations + 1 cross-id merge (C0242 → C0196, `shared email meenareddymail.com`); master rows 499; every loser evidenced by shared email in the registry.

questions.title: Repeated customers: same person?

questions.headline: The join key is `norm_id` = strip + UPPER + remove spaces/dashes. Normalisation changes 23 customer rows' form but distinct ids stay 500 before and after — no customer is double-counted by spelling; the order side's 693 spellings collapse to 482 ids (variants of the same people). The only count reduction (520 rows → 499) comes from D03 email merges, not from id normalisation.
questions.method: `norm_id` is applied to customer ids; distinct counts and changed-row counts are compared raw vs normalised, and order-side spellings are counted the same way.

result.value: customer rows changed by normalisation 23 (`C0032 `→`C0032`, `c0010`→`C0010`, `C-0176`→`C0176`); distinct raw 500 = distinct normalised 500; order-side customer_id: 693 raw spellings → 482 normalised ids.

questions.title: Case/spacing/dash customer variants

questions.headline: The gap has three parts: 20 customers registered but never ordered (master without orders); 3 unmatched order-side groups — C9999 (144 rows, unknown id → quarantined by R01), 14 rows under loser id C0242 (remapped to C0196 by D03 in the clean layer — 0 remain), and 60 rows with no customer id at all. Nothing else is unresolved.
questions.method: Master ids are matched against distinct customer ids in the raw orders with both sides normalised; order-side id groups with no master match are counted with their row volumes.

result.value: master 499; with orders 479; without orders 20; order-side ids 482 (479 matched); unmatched — C9999 144 rows, C0242 14 rows (remapped), blank 60 rows.

questions.title: Customers with and without orders

questions.headline: All 21 groups required a decision and were resolved by the same email rule; excluding placeholder emails (42) prevents false merges, since many customers legitimately share `NA`/blank. Dependency: D03 must run before order-level dedup because remapped ids change D01/D02/D05 matching — rule order is load-bearing.
questions.method: Customers are grouped by lowercased email with placeholders excluded; every group larger than one is a merge decision, and D03's evidence strings cross-check the same groups.

result.value: shared-email groups 21; extra rows merged 21; 20 same-id / 1 cross-id (C0242/C0196); placeholder emails excluded 42 (32 empty + 10 placeholder); example group: `[email masked]` → C0218 (Bengaluru) + C0218 (Pune).

questions.title: Shared email addresses

questions.headline: No two product rows share a name (or a normalised id), so nothing needs merging; the evidence for the 30 products is 30 distinct names — duplicate-name handling is a non-issue in this catalogue.
questions.method: Product names are compared case-insensitively across rows; D04's comparison (name + category + price) only activates when normalized ids collide.

result.value: names appearing on more than one row: none; 30 rows, 30 distinct names; D04 collisions 0.

questions.title: Shared product names

questions.headline: No id repeats, so no per-repeat action was needed; five ids are formatting variants (`p09`, `P-10`, `P-20`, `P-26`, `P-30`) that normalise to ids not otherwise present, so they neither merge nor conflict. Product count is unchanged: 30 → 30.
questions.method: Repeated product_id rows are counted, `norm_id` variants are listed, and the D04 registry is checked for merges or CONFLICT rows.

result.value: repeated product_ids 0; D04 registry rows 0 (merges 0, CONFLICT 0); normalised variants 5 (`p09`→P09, `P-10`→P10, `P-20`→P20, `P-26`→P26, `P-30`→P30); products 30 → 30.

questions.title: Repeated product_ids

questions.headline: The survivor's city is trusted (earliest signup) and the loser's city is dropped — 18 of 21 merges had differing cities, and merged-away occurrences are single digits per city (Pune 5, Bengaluru 4, chennai 2, BLR 2, Mysuru 2, Madras 1, bengaluru 1, Hyderabad 1), so no city disappears. Raw spelling variety (8 distinct case-folded spellings: BLR/Bangalore/Bengaluru, Madras/Chennai, ...) is handled at the standardised layer (`city_std`); the master keeps one city per survivor.

It becomes equivalent iff the ORDER BY is total (unique key last, e.g. order_id COLLATE C). Past the size threshold the planner switches the LATERAL to a hashed/merged per-group scan, which surfaces the arbitrariness.

questions.headline: Range split at midpoint 2025-05-27 (< mid vs >= mid); the second half takes the extra day on odd spans. >5pp movers: 2.
questions.method: Q111: categories whose order share moved >5pp between halves.
questions.title: Category share shift >5pp

questions.headline: Canonical ordering (product_a < product_b) counts each unordered pair once; without it every pair double-counts (a,b)+(b,a).
questions.method: Q112: top-5 product pairs same customer+date (canonical order).
questions.title: Top-5 product pairs

questions.headline: Minimum-5 filter first (p90 = 66.00%); filtering after would let 1-order 100%-cancel customers set the bar.
questions.method: Q113: customers above p90 cancel/return rate (min 5 orders).
questions.title: Above p90 cancel rate

questions.headline: SUM over quantity never expands rows. Recursive unit-row expansion is O(units) memory for an identical total; it can only differ through float rounding or bad-quantity handling.
questions.method: Q114: units per product per month via SUM(quantity).
questions.title: Units per product per month

questions.headline: COUNT(DISTINCT) cannot sit inside a window frame portably, so the distinct count is a subquery and LAG runs over its months.
questions.method: Q115: months with fewer distinct completed cities than prior.
questions.title: Months losing city coverage

questions.headline: G = 2*sum(i*x_i)/(n*sum) - (n+1)/n on ascending values; assumes non-negative values and one observation per customer. Near 1 = one customer takes nearly everything: target them, diversify the rest.
questions.method: Q116: Gini of completed value across customers per city.
questions.title: Gini of value across customers

questions.headline: Tie-break (count DESC, payment ASC): 51 differ. Reversed name tiebreak: 47; differs for 4.
questions.method: Q117: most-frequent vs most-recent payment_mode (tie: count,name).
questions.title: Usual vs latest payment mode

questions.headline: NULL, negative and >7 values sit in outside_or_invalid (counted, never averaged away); bands use closed integer intervals.
questions.method: Q118: delivery_days bands per city with shares.
questions.title: Delivery-day bands per city

questions.headline: Negative lags (first order before signup, n=265) excluded from medians and counted. Shortest cohort: 2024-08 (54.0 days).
questions.method: Q119: signup-month cohort with shortest median signup->first-order.
questions.title: Fastest signup cohort

questions.headline: The view projects line_value only; a query over it cannot return raw unit_price_paid text. The test cannot prove the base table is protected (grants, replicas, logs still expose it).
questions.method: Q120: completed-values view exposes no raw price text.
questions.title: Completed-values view, no raw text

questions.headline: CROSS JOIN grid left-joined to sales; missing cells are zero, not absent. Structural vs data gap: join the full order set (any status) - a combo present there but absent in completed is a fulfilment gap; absent everywhere is structural/assortment.
questions.method: Q121: city x category combos with no completed orders.
questions.title: Empty city x category cells

questions.headline: DENSE_RANK ties share rank 1, so tied months add every tied product; ROW_NUMBER would keep one and shrink the list.
questions.method: Q122: products rank-1 in monthly qty within category, >=3 months.
questions.title: Rank-1 products, 3+ months

questions.headline: Blank/UNMAPPED categories: division ignores them (needs every real category), HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT) can match the wrong total if blanks are counted. No blanks here, so both agree.
questions.method: Q123: customers buying every catalogue category (division vs HAVING).
questions.title: Customers buying every category

questions.headline: Lines with no catalogue price excluded (counted in docs, not the rate). Doubling = share >= 2x prior month; NULL prior never flags.
questions.method: Q124: monthly share of lines >5% off catalogue; doubling flagged.
questions.title: Off-catalogue months doubling

questions.headline: CTEs: completed, city totals, ranked cities, category shares; window ranks cities; LATERAL fetches each top category; GROUPING SETS labels subtotals; anti-join drops non-completed cities. At 10x rows the per-city sort spills first (work_mem), then the self-join.
questions.method: Q125: top-3 cities + top category + share (4 CTEs, window, LATERAL,
questions.title: Top-3 cities mega query

rules.name: Valid Price
rules.predicate: unit_price_paid is positive and near the catalogue price

rules.name: Valid Discount
rules.predicate: discount parses to a fraction in 0..1

rules.name: Valid Status
rules.predicate: order_status is not MISSING or UNMAPPED

rules.name: Valid Delivery Days
rules.predicate: delivery_days is an integer in 0..30 for Delivered

rules.name: Inventory Feasibility
rules.predicate: quantity does not exceed recorded stock_qty
